summary: This document specifies how to send IPv6 packets over ITU-T G.9959 networks, which are low-power wireless networks used for things like home automation. It defines the frame format and how to form link-local and stateless autoconfigured IPv6 addresses.

eli5.summary: Tiny wireless gadgets in a house, like sensors and switches, can learn to speak internet language. This document tells them how to wrap their messages and make their own addresses.

questions: how does g.9959 form an ipv6 address
does g.9959 ipv6 need duplicate address detection
subtitle: How tiny home-automation radios carry IPv6 packets, and how they build their own IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: ITU-T G.9959 networks are low-power personal area networks with very small frames and 8-bit node identifiers, so ordinary IPv6 framing and addressing do not fit them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adapts the 6LoWPAN approach of RFC 4944 to G.9959: IPv6 packets ride in a 6LoWPAN frame with header compression, and a node builds its interface identifier from its 8-bit NodeID.
tldr.outcome: G.9959 devices can speak IPv6 with compact headers and addresses that need no duplicate address detection. The RFC requires G.9959 shared network key security.

today: RFC 7428 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of IPv6 over G.9959 networks.

sections.title: IPv6 on Low-Power G.9959 Networks
sections.content:
The ITU-T G.9959 recommendation targets low-power Personal Area Networks (PANs). RFC 7428 defines the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over such networks, and how to form IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on them.

The general approach is to adapt elements of RFC 4944 to G.9959. G.9959 itself provides a Segmentation and Reassembly (SAR) layer for datagrams larger than one MAC frame. The document limits the use of RFC 6775 to prefix and Context ID assignment.

Mesh-under and route-over routing protocol specifications are out of scope, though the frame format may be used by routing protocols such as RPL.
sections.eli5: Tiny home gadgets use a special radio language. This document is the translation guide that lets them also speak internet language.

sections.title: G.9959 Parameters for IPv6 Transport
sections.content:
G.9959 assigns a 32-bit HomeID to a network and an 8-bit NodeID to each node. The HomeID represents an IPv6 subnet identified by one or more prefixes. A host MUST build its link-local address from the link-layer-derived interface identifier, which helps header compression.

A node may support the M flag of the Router Advertisement. If it does not, or the flag is 0, the node MUST use link-layer-derived addressing. If the flag is 1, the node MUST use DHCPv6-based addressing and comply fully with RFC 6775.

IPv6 multicast packets MUST be carried via G.9959 broadcast, with the network's HomeID and the broadcast NodeID 0xff. Packets MUST be sent using transmission profile R3 or higher. G.9959 segmentation handles payloads up to 1350 octets, and with mandatory link-layer security an R3 frame fits 6LoWPAN datagrams of up to 130 octets without segmentation.

HomeIDs and NodeIDs are handed out by a network controller, so their validity depends on network membership. A single controller is a single point of failure, and high-reliability deployments may want a redundant controller.
sections.eli5: Every house network has a street name and every gadget has a house number. The gadgets build their internet address from that house number, and a broadcast shout is how they send a message to everybody.

sections.title: The 6LoWPAN Frame Format
sections.content:
The 6LoWPAN encapsulation is carried as payload in the G.9959 MAC PDU. IPv6 header compression from RFC 6282 MUST be supported. Generic Header Compression from RFC 7400 MAY be supported, and a node using it MUST probe its peers first.

The frame starts with a 6LoWPAN Command Class byte that MUST be 0x4F, assigned by the ITU-T. Frames with another value MUST be ignored by 6LoWPAN protocols. A Dispatch field follows, then a type-specific header. Only one dispatch value applies here: pattern 01 1xxxxx, the 6LoWPAN_IPHC header.

The header stack is not meant to be a general-purpose extensibility mechanism.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a secret handshake byte that says this is an internet message. Messages that do not start with it are ignored.

sections.title: Addressing and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
A NodeID is mapped into an interface identifier of the form 0000:00ff:fe00:YYXX. XX carries the NodeID and YY is a byte chosen by the node, defaulting to zero. A node MAY use other YY values to run several IPv6 interfaces. A node MUST NOT compute a NodeID from an IID whose first 6 bytes do not match this format; RFC 6775 address resolution applies instead.

The link-local address is the prefix fe80::/64 plus this IID, with the Universal/Local bit set to zero. The same IID MUST be used for ULA and globally routable addresses.

Neighbor Discovery uses a Source/Target Link-layer Address option with Length 1 that carries the NodeID. In route-over networks, hosts MUST use RFC 6775 address registration. Mesh-under networks MUST NOT use it for compliant IIDs and MUST NOT use Duplicate Address Detection, because G.9959 inclusion already makes a NodeID unique per HomeID.

Context ID handling has special rules. An expired CID MUST NOT be reused immediately, and an RA Router Lifetime of 0xFFFF means infinite lifetime, which ABRs MUST NOT use.
sections.eli5: A gadget makes its internet address by putting its small house number into a fixed pattern. Since house numbers never repeat in one network, nobody needs to check for twins.

sections.title: Header Compression Substitutions
sections.content:
IPv6 header compression per RFC 6282 MUST be implemented. The RFC does not copy that text; it lists substitutions to apply: replace 802.15.4 with G.9959, replace the 802.15.4 short address with <Interface><G.9959 NodeID>, and replace the 802.15.4 PAN ID with the G.9959 HomeID.

Where a 16-bit address is needed, it is formed by prepending an Interface label byte to the NodeID. If the Interface number is zero, all IPv6 address bytes may be elided when the address can be rebuilt from the link-layer destination. The 64-bit 802.15.4 address details do not apply.

Appendix A walks through a sample UDP packet bit by bit, showing a link-layer-derived IID compressed down to a 16-bit value.
sections.eli5: To save space, the sender leaves out anything the receiver can guess, like parts of the address it can rebuild from the house number.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Building IIDs from 8-bit NodeIDs keeps them unique in the network, but gives no protection against forgery. Neighbor Discovery on G.9959 may face the threats in RFC 3756, and mesh routing adds more. G.9959 nodes MUST use link-layer security with a shared key; G.9959 relies on AES for authentication and encryption and uses challenge-response handshaking against replay. Devices that talk outside their subnet are expected to use IPsec or TLS end to end.

On privacy, link-layer-derived IIDs are static, but the risk is limited because the link-layer address is only 8 bits. DHCPv6 can decouple addresses from the link layer, but non-link-layer-derived IIDs cannot be compressed and need address registration. Frequent prefix changes also mean more Context ID updates, which can affect battery life of sleeping nodes.
sections.eli5: All the gadgets share a secret key so outsiders cannot listen in or fake messages. Changing addresses often protects privacy but costs the tiny batteries more work.

fields.desc: A header determined by the Dispatch value.
